To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the use of a 3D camera is crucial for accurate sorting, (2) the combination of a convolutional neural network and a support vector machine yields the most accurate classification results, and (3) the system is robust to the influence of lighting conditions, camera orientation, and wood waste size.
a vision-based sorting system for MDF and grade B wood is possible and has been successfully deployed in industry.

(1) a computer vision-based system for the sorting of MDF, OSF and particleboard material from grade A wood waste is feasible, (2) this system is robust and reliable enough to be deployed in industry (TRL 9) and (3) the return on investment is less than one year.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following three main contributions: 1.
the development of a vision-based sorting system that can separate MDF, OSD and other particleboard from quality wood in an automated and reliable way.
a vision-based solution that can be used in the wood recycling industry to separate MDF, OSBD and other particleboard from grade A wood waste.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our vision-based wood waste sorting system is a reliable, cheap and accurate solution for separating MDF, OSD and other grade B wood from quality wood.
the system presented in this paper can be used to sort wood waste in order to separate grade B wood from grade A wood with an accuracy of 99%.
our system can be used in the industry to sort grade B wood from quality wood with a high accuracy, and at a high throughput rate, which is a significant improvement over the manual sorting process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed an industry ready solution for the wood waste sorting problem, with a very short return on investment.
we were able to build a system that can sort wood waste in real time and with a very high degree of accuracy.
the proposed system has a very high sorting performance, which is very close to the performance of human operators, but with much less effort and at a fraction of the cost.
The main takeaway from our work is that
computer vision is an enabling technology for many applications in the wood industry.

computer vision and machine-learning-based solutions can be successfully integrated into industrial settings, provided that they are designed with industrial requirements in mind from the very beginning of the design process.

state-of-the-art techniques from computer vision and machine-learning can be used to develop an industry ready system, which is able to process 7.5 tonnes of wood waste per hours, with a very low false positive and false negative rate.
